name: Jouvence Blue
lede: Jouvence Blue is a dark greenish blue that Ridgway standardized in 1912, repeated by Maerz and Paul in 1930, and rare in our painting archive.

sections.title: Two records, one blue
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places Jouvence Blue on plate XX, hue 43 prime, tone k, and again on plate VII, hue 41 [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary repeats it on plate 29, swatch L3, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as a moderate bluish green, block 164 [1]. Jouvence is French for rejuvenation; whether that sense inspired this particular blue is undocumented in the sources we checked [1].

Its closest named neighbor in our library is [[deep-aqua|Deep Aqua]]; the nearest common color word is [[petrol|Petrol]], about six units away in CIEDE2000, and it sits in our Blues family between [[blue]] and [[teal]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Jouvence Blue is rare in our painting archive: a color within six units of it covers at least five percent of the canvas in 33 of our 23,781 paintings, 0.14 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens narrows that to nine [2]. That ranks it rarer than 69 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 5 of 8,345 paintings, at just 0.1 percent of that century's paintings, 1.2 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1445, by Domenico Veneziano, 467 years before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a dye that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

questions.q: Where does Ridgway's nomenclature place Jouvence Blue?
True or false: our sources confirm the name Jouvence Blue was chosen for the French meaning 'rejuvenation'.
